text.brief: On July 14, 1982, James Lilley of the American Institute in Taiwan carried six assurances to President Chiang Ching-kuo in Taipei.
text.record: The United States had set no date to end arms sales to Taiwan and would not consult the Party on them. It would not mediate, revise the Taiwan Relations Act, change its position on sovereignty or press Taipei to negotiate. Five weeks later the Joint Communiqué of August 17 said Washington intended to reduce arms sales over time ([Reagan Library: United States-China Joint Communique on United States Arms Sales to Taiwan, August 17, 1982](https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/archives/speech/united-states-china-joint-communique-united-states-arms-sales-taiwan); [American Institute in Taiwan: U.S.-PRC Joint Communique (1982)](https://www.ait.org.tw/u-s-prc-joint-communique-1982/)). Ronald Reagan wrote in a memo the same day that any reduction depended on the Party's commitment to a peaceful solution. The memo stayed classified until 2020.
text.reading: The Party reads the communiqué with its condition removed and cites it as a pledge to end arms sales, which is Stratagem 25. One president kept the condition in writing, and that page gave later officials a text to stand on.
text.gapText: Data Architecture. The condition that governed the policy sat in a classified file for 38 years while the Party's reading ran in public.
text.fix: Publish the conditions of every commitment with the commitment itself.
